name: Marcella of Rome
knownFor: A Roman widow who, by Jerome's account, was the first highborn lady at Rome to take up the monastic life openly, and to whom Roman Christians turned with questions on Scripture.
dates: Died at Rome a few days after the city was taken in 410 (the year given in the notes to W. H. Fremantle's English edition of Jerome); her birth year is not given
place: Rome, where Jerome says she "has her abode upon the Aventine"
role: Widow, ascetic and student of Scripture

traces: Monastic life for women at Rome, which Jerome says she took up when no highborn lady there had yet dared "publicly to call herself a nun"; Eustochium was trained in her cell.
The Roman condemnation of the Origenists, which Jerome credits to her: "She it was who originated the condemnation of the heretics."
remembered: Jerome of Strido wrote her memorial two years after her death, in a letter to her friend Principia, and calls her "Marcella the glory of her native Rome."
Seventeen of Jerome's letters to her are held. Many answer her questions on Scripture, several of them on Hebrew words.

uncertain: Her life is known from Jerome alone, chiefly his memorial letter to Principia, which is a friend's praise. Nothing of hers survives in her own words.
Jerome was not at Rome when it was taken. He tells the beating as what he heard from "holy men" who were there, and much of it as what "is said".

Jerome was a party to the Origenist quarrel at Rome, and he admits that readers may think him "giving vent to my own rancour." The notes in W. H. Fremantle's English edition, not Jerome's letter, name the translator of Origen's book as Rufinus of Aquileia.
The Library holds no account of Marcella from the side of those she opposed.
